Montana Empire kit PHP components staged on web infrastructure AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the Montana Empire kit's distinctive server-side PHP files (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php) being written to disk or requested over HTTP, indicating the postal-service phishing clone is being staged or is live on infrastructure you can see. Article-specific because these three filenames are the kit's internal component names, not generic web paths. Rationale: Pivots on the three exact PHP component names Unit 42/CyberPress attribute to the Montana Empire kit (panel_track.php, verify_api.php, mentalite.php); these are non-generic internal filenames, so a file-create or IIS request for them is high-fidelity for kit staging on visible infra. Cross-checked against: • https://origin-unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://cyberpress.org/ai-hallucinated-domain-theft/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named panel_track.php in an unrelated in-house web app
  • Pen-test / red-team dropping a lookalike phishing kit during an authorised exercise
  • WAF or scanner replaying kit URIs against your site (request hits with 404s, no file on disk)
  • Security researcher unpacking the kit ZIP on an analysis host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the hit is a file-write (kit staged locally) vs an inbound IIS request (external probing); check the folder path, writing process, and HTTP status. 2) Contain: if written to your web root, take the site offline / remove the files and preserve a forensic copy; if inbound-only, block the source IP and confirm no 200 responses. 3) Hunt: look for the kit ZIP hash on the same host, outbound connections to api.telegram.org (kit C2), and any web-shell-style process (php/w3wp spawning cmd/powershell).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("panel_track.php","verify_api.php","mentalite.php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("panel_track.php","verify_api.php","mentalite.php")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding-assistant egress to first-seen external domain (phantom squatting) AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the article's core TTP: an AI coding assistant / agent process (Cursor, VS Code+Copilot, Windsurf, Ollama, etc.) making an outbound connection or DNS query to an external domain the org has never seen before — the moment an LLM-hallucinated, adversary-pre-registered 'phantom' domain is fetched with zero reputation. Article-specific because it scopes rare-domain egress to AI-assistant parent processes, the exact trust surface Unit 42 describes. Rationale: No hard domain IOC exists (Unit 42 redacted the live phantom domains and the build-notifier[.]io URL is explicitly illustrative), so this targets the behavioural core of the article — an AI dev-assistant binary reaching a zero-reputation, never-before-seen external domain — via a 30-day leftanti baseline scoped to named AI-client processes. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/phantom-squatting-uses-ai-hallucinated.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately adopting a new SaaS/API the AI assistant correctly recommended (real, newly-used domain)
  • AI extension auto-update or telemetry endpoint not yet in baseline
  • First use of a new package registry mirror or docs CDN
  • Newly onboarded host with no 30-day baseline generating many first-seen domains
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".github.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".githubcopilot.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".openai.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".anthropic.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".ollama.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".visualstudio.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the first-seen domain's registration age (WHOIS) and reputation; a domain registered within days that matches a brand's naming pattern is the phantom-squat signal, whereas an established SaaS domain is benign. 2) Contain: if the domain is newly-registered/unreputed, block it at DNS/proxy and warn the developer not to hardcode the URL; capture what data the assistant sent. 3) Hunt: search all hosts for the same domain, check whether the URL was committed into source/config, and review the AI-assistant session for other hallucinated endpoints.
let AiClients = dynamic(["cursor.exe","code.exe","windsurf.exe","ollama.exe","copilot.exe","continue.exe","claude.exe"]);
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AiClients)
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AiClients)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RemoteUrl
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Hosts=dcount(DeviceName), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 5) by RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let AiClients = dynamic(["cursor.exe","code.exe","windsurf.exe","ollama.exe","copilot.exe","continue.exe","claude.exe"]);
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AiClients)
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Hosts=dcount(DeviceName), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 5) by RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\\cursor.exe OR *\\Cursor.exe) OR @Image:(*\\code.exe OR *\\Code.exe) OR @Image:(*\\windsurf.exe OR *\\Windsurf.exe) OR @Image:(*\\ollama.exe OR *\\Ollama.exe) OR @Image:(*\\continue.exe OR *\\Continue.exe))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Warns Poisoned MCP Tool Descriptions Can Make AI Agents Leak Data

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 10 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

New Microsoft&nbsp;research&nbsp;shows how attackers can hijack AI agents that act on a user's behalf, using nothing more than a poisoned tool description to make the agent quietly hand over company data to an outsider. The trick is that the agent never breaks a rule. Every step looks routine, so in a default setup no alarm may fire. The work comes from Microsoft Incident Response and its

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious postmark-mcp npm package install or on-disk presence (supply-chain MCP server) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network/DNS IOC sweep for postmark-mcp exfil domain giftshop.club · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Covert BCC email exfiltration to giftshop.club via trojanized postmark-mcp · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Malicious postmark-mcp npm package install or on-disk presence (supply-chain MCP server) AIDelivery High
Hunts installation or filesystem presence of the trojanized postmark-mcp MCP server (v1.0.16+, publisher phanpak) that the Microsoft article cites as the first real-world malicious MCP server. Catches the supply-chain entry point before the agent ever runs the poisoned tool. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious package name postmark-mcp confirmed by Koi Security/Snyk/Postmark; any install of this impersonating package is high-fidelity since Postmark never published it and v1.0.16+ is confirmed backdoored. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://postmarkapp.com/blog/information-regarding-malicious-postmark-mcp-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1199
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately testing/evaluating postmark-mcp before the malicious disclosure
  • Internal mirror/proxy npm cache replaying the package name in audit tooling
  • Security researcher reproducing the Koi finding in a sandbox
  • SBOM/dependency-scanning tool string-matching the package name in its own logs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ('mssense.exe','sentinelagent.exe') and not (FolderPath has 'sandbox' or DeviceName has 'sec-research')
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installed version via package-lock.json / node_modules/postmark-mcp/package.json — v1.0.16 and later are backdoored. Identify the host, user, and whether the MCP server actually ran. 2) Contain: uninstall the package, block npm publisher 'phanpak', and isolate any host/agent that sent live email through it; rotate Postmark API tokens and any credentials ever emailed via the agent. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound mail logs for BCC to giftshop.club (UC2) and sweep all hosts for the node_modules\postmark-mcp path and the domain across DNS/proxy.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has 'postmark-mcp'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source='ProcessCreate', Detail=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath ),
( DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @'node_modules\postmark-mcp' or FolderPath contains 'node_modules/postmark-mcp'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source='FileWrite', Detail=FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath )
| where AccountName !endswith '$'
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has 'postmark-mcp'
| where SubjectUserName !endswith '$'
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious postmark-mcp npm Package Installation
id: 9f2a4b7c-1d3e-4f5a-8b6c-2e1d0a9f8c7b
status: experimental
description: Detects installation of the trojanized postmark-mcp npm package (v1.0.16+, publisher phanpak) that BCCs all agent-sent email to phan@giftshop.club.
references:
  - https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-warns-poisoned-mcp-tool.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains: 'postmark-mcp'
  install_ctx:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'install'
      - 'npx'
      - ' add '
  condition: selection and install_ctx
falsepositives:
  - Developer evaluating the package before it was flagged malicious
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:*postmark-mcp*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/postmark-mcp/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*postmark-mcp*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*postmark-mcp*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Covert BCC email exfiltration to giftshop.club via trojanized postmark-mcp AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual exfiltration channel of the postmark-mcp backdoor: every email the agent sends is silently BCC'd to phan@giftshop.club. Surfaces any outbound mail with a recipient/BCC in the giftshop.club domain. Rationale: giftshop.club / phan@giftshop.club is the confirmed BCC exfil sink for postmark-mcp v1.0.16, corroborated by Koi, Snyk, Qualys and Postmark's advisory; any mail to that domain is a direct true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/ • https://threatprotect.qualys.com/2025/09/30/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-exploited-in-attack/
ATT&CKT1041 T1114.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate business contact who genuinely uses a giftshop.club address (verify against directory)
  • Marketing/transactional bulk mail accidentally addressed to the domain
  • Threat-intel detonation/sandbox that replays the IOC in a test tenant
  • Phishing-simulation platform seeding the known-bad domain
Suppression filter
| where not (EmailDirection == 'Inbound')
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull every message in the hit set, identify the sending mailbox/agent identity and whether messages contain sensitive content (invoices, credentials). Confirm giftshop.club is not a known legitimate partner. 2) Contain: create a transport rule blocking mail to giftshop.club, suspend the implicated agent/service identity, and remove postmark-mcp from the sending host; rotate Postmark tokens. 3) Hunt: enumerate all mailboxes/agents that ever sent via postmark-mcp, scope total exfil volume, and check for other phanpak-published packages in the environment.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RecipientEmailAddress has 'giftshop.club' or SenderFromDomain =~ 'giftshop.club' or SenderMailFromDomain =~ 'giftshop.club'
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, EmailDirection, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload has 'Exchange'
| where Recipients has 'giftshop.club' or P2RecipientList has 'giftshop.club'
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, UserId, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender, P2Sender, Recipients, P2RecipientList, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.message_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.recipient="*giftshop.club*" by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.message_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Network/DNS IOC sweep for postmark-mcp exfil domain giftshop.club AICommand & Control Medium
Cross-telemetry sweep for any host resolving or connecting to giftshop.club, the attacker domain behind the postmark-mcp backdoor. Catch-all in case the domain is reused for web callbacks or appears in proxy/DNS where mail telemetry is blind. Rationale: giftshop.club is the confirmed attacker domain (multi-source); a pure-IOC domain sweep across DNS/proxy/network is a cheap catch-all that complements the email-BCC detection where mail telemetry is unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.koi.ai/blog/postmark-mcp-npm-malicious-backdoor-email-theft • https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/29/postmark_mcp_server_code_hijacked/ • https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-mcp-server-on-npm-postmark-mcp-harvests-emails/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed connectors that beacon IOC domains for reputation lookups
  • Sandbox/detonation infrastructure resolving the known-bad domain
  • Security awareness or phishing-sim platform referencing the domain
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ telemetry logging blocked lookups (already mitigated)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ('msmpeng.exe','mssense.exe','sentinelagent.exe','filebeat.exe')
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the initiating process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) — confirm it is not a security tool doing reputation lookups. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block giftshop.club at DNS and proxy, isolate the host if a non-security process initiated the lookup, and check that host for postmark-mcp. 3) Hunt: correlate with outbound mail-BCC hits (UC2) and package-install hits (UC1) on the same host, and add giftshop.club to the org blocklist/TI watchlist.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has 'giftshop.club'
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
( ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has 'giftshop.club' | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, Indicator=DnsQuery, Source='DNS' ),
( DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has 'giftshop.club' | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=ClientIP, SrcHostname=Computer, Indicator=Name, Source='DnsEvents' ),
( CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where RequestURL has 'giftshop.club' or DestinationHostName has 'giftshop.club' | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, SrcHostname=SourceHostName, Indicator=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName), Source='Proxy' )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

RustDuck Botnet Rebuilds in Rust to Hijack Routers and Servers for DDoS

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 12 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A new two-stage malware family called RustDuck is hijacking home routers, IP cameras, Android boxes, and poorly secured servers, then stitching them into a network built to knock websites and online services offline. Researchers at QiAnXin's&nbsp;XLab&nbsp;have tracked it since February 2026, and say the real story is not how big it is today, but how fast it is changing. The end goal is a

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] RustDuck worm-style outbound scanning on Telnet/SSH/ADB ports · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] RustDuck-targeted CVE exposure across managed devices · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] RustDuck two-stage loader file/execution by SHA1 hash · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] RustDuck C2/delivery infrastructure callback to 176.65.139.204 · [LLM] RustDuck duckdns.org and dynamic-DNS C2 domain resolution · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
RustDuck C2/delivery infrastructure callback to 176.65.139.204 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host in the estate that talks to RustDuck's busiest implant-delivery/C2 address 176.65.139.204. XLab flags this IP as the most active source spreading the two-stage RustDuck loader, so any inbound-from or outbound-to this address on a managed device is a strong compromise or exploit-attempt signal. Rationale: 176.65.139.204 is the single concrete network IOC in the article and is confirmed by XLab's report as the busiest RustDuck delivery source; a discrete IP match is inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against the XLab blog IOC list. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/rustduck-en/ • https://securityaffairs.com/194556/malware/rustduck-the-botnet-thats-still-small-but-engineering-like-it-plans-to-grow.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel/blocklist appliance or sandbox intentionally probing the IP for enrichment
  • A security researcher in the org detonating the sample in a lab that egresses through the corporate proxy
  • Shared bulletproof-hosting IP that also fronts an unrelated benign service (low likelihood for this address)
  • NAT/proxy egress collapsing many hosts to one SourceIP in firewall logs, obscuring the true origin
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "SentinelOne")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the internal host and the initiating process; confirm whether the connection succeeded (ActionType/DeviceAction) and its direction. Pull the process tree and any file the process wrote in the prior hour. 2) CONTAIN: block 176.65.139.204 at the perimeter, isolate the host (or reboot/reimage the IoT/router if it is unmanaged network gear), and rotate any credentials that were exposed on that device's Telnet/SSH/web-admin. 3) HUNT: sweep for the RustDuck loader hashes (UC 'loader SHA1') and duckdns C2 domains (UC 'C2 domains') across all hosts, and review whether the device is one of the CVE-vulnerable models in the exposure hunt.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "176.65.139.204"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "176.65.139.204" or SourceIP == "176.65.139.204"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RustDuck two-stage loader file/execution by SHA1 hash AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on the presence or execution of the four RustDuck loader variants by their SHA1 hashes from XLab. The loader decrypts and unpacks the heavier Rust core, so a hash hit on any managed Linux/Windows server or endpoint means RustDuck stage-1 landed on that host. Rationale: Four SHA1 loader hashes are published in XLab's IOC list (referenced by the article's 'file hashes' line); a hash match has essentially zero false positives. Emitted for both file-write and process-exec so a dropped-but-not-yet-run loader is still caught. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/rustduck-en/
ATT&CKT1105 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sample intentionally staged in a malware-analysis VM that ships EDR telemetry
  • Hash re-use in a threat-hunting training/detonation range
  • Backup/AV quarantine copies of the same file re-scanned generating file events (not executions)
  • Extremely unlikely benign SHA1 collision
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !has "/malware-lab/"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm whether this was a file write only or an actual execution; capture the full path and the parent process. For IoT/router gear surfaced via Linux MDE, check whether it was reachable from the internet. 2) CONTAIN: kill and quarantine the binary, isolate the host, and preserve a copy for IR. Block the loader hashes org-wide via custom indicator. 3) HUNT: from the same host pivot to outbound connections (176.65.139.204 and duckdns C2 UCs) and to any /tmp or web-writable staging directory to find the unpacked Rust core.

| order by Timestamp desc

RustDuck duckdns.org and dynamic-DNS C2 domain resolution AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS lookups / connections to the exact RustDuck C2 FQDNs published by XLab, including six *.duckdns.org subdomains plus five other free dynamic-DNS/registrar domains. Named FQDNs make this far higher-fidelity than a generic 'contacts duckdns' rule. Rationale: The six duckdns subdomains and five other C2 FQDNs are taken verbatim from XLab's IOC list (the article names duckdns.org as the C2 backbone but does not list the subdomains). Exact-FQDN matching avoids the FP problem of allow/deny-listing all of duckdns.org. Datadog left empty: no DNS-query log source is available in this tenant's Datadog schema. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/rustduck-en/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal user who independently registered one of these duckdns subdomains for a hobby project (very unlikely given the random strings)
  • Passive-DNS / TI enrichment tooling resolving the domains for research
  • Sinkhole redirection after takedown still generating resolution logs
  • Web-content-filter appliance pre-resolving domains from a blocklist feed
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the resolving host and the process that triggered the lookup; determine if the resolution was followed by an actual connection to the returned IP. 2) CONTAIN: sinkhole/block all eleven FQDNs at the resolver and perimeter, isolate the host, and treat it as RustDuck-infected pending forensics. 3) HUNT: because RustDuck rotates C2 and can push 'switch to new control servers' commands, pivot on the resolved A-record IPs and on 176.65.139.204 to discover additional infrastructure, and scan for the loader hashes.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (c2)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2 = dynamic(["igmc.duckdns.org","qewqewqewqtq.duckdns.org","qewqewqewqtqthree.duckdns.org","qewqewqewqtqtwo.duckdns.org","dhdsjsdjxc.duckdns.org","fcfrfxrfrsfs5f.duckdns.org","gayporn.twilightparadox.com","bigniggadick.ignorelist.com","ilovefemboy.mooo.com","disciplinenahidwin.st","criminalcloudflare.online"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any (c2)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, IPAddresses, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RustDuck-targeted CVE exposure across managed devices AIExploitation High
Attack-surface hunt that surfaces every managed device carrying one of the four historical CVEs RustDuck weaponises (Huawei HG532, D-Link DIR-823X, Totolink X6000R, Apache CouchDB). Prioritises internet-facing and end-of-life gear for removal/patching before the botnet reaches it. Rationale: The four CVE IDs are stated verbatim in the article and confirmed in the XLab report. A TVM posture query is the cleanest way to close 'the doors it walks through' (the article's explicit defensive advice), and it prioritises EOL/internet-facing devices CISA advises pulling from service (DIR-823X). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/rustduck-en/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/rustduck-botnet-rapidly-evolves-with-migration-to-rust
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM version-inference flagging a device that has a vendor backport fixing the CVE without a version bump
  • A decommissioned router still in inventory but no longer network-reachable
  • A lab/test device intentionally kept vulnerable
  • Duplicate device records inflating counts (mitigated by arg_max per DeviceId)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: rank hits by IsInternetFacing then severity; confirm which are supported (CouchDB has fixed releases) vs EOL (DIR-823X, Totolink X6000R never patched). 2) CONTAIN: for supported software, patch to the fixed release; for EOL gear follow CISA guidance and remove it from service or move remote-admin (Telnet/SSH/ADB/web-UI) off the public internet. 3) HUNT: for any device that was internet-facing, retro-hunt the C2 IP, C2 domains and loader hashes to confirm it was not already recruited before patching.

| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp,*) by DeviceId | project DeviceId, IsInternetFacing) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2017-17215","CVE-2025-29635","CVE-2024-1781","CVE-2018-8007")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

RustDuck worm-style outbound scanning on Telnet/SSH/ADB ports AIDelivery Medium
Behavioural hunt for a compromised host propagating RustDuck: a single internal source fanning out to many distinct public IPs on the botnet's spread ports (Telnet 23, SSH 22, Android Debug Bridge 5555). This is the propagation shape RustDuck uses to brute-force credentials and hit exposed ADB, distinct from the IOC-match UCs. Rationale: The article names weak-password Telnet/SSH login guessing and exposed ADB as RustDuck's primary spread vectors; a host fanning out to 50+ external hosts on ports 22/23/5555 in an hour is the propagation fingerprint. The 50-target/1h threshold flags scanning while tolerating a handful of legit admin SSH sessions. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/rustduck-en/ • https://gbhackers.com/rustduck-botnet-targets-iot-devices/
ATT&CKT1046 T1110
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Nmap) sweeping external assets
  • A CI/CD or config-management host (Ansible/Salt) pushing to many SSH targets
  • A backup or file-transfer server with a large external SFTP fleet
  • A jump host used by admins to reach many customer devices on SSH
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus.exe","nmap.exe","ansible","salt-minion","scp","sftp","plink.exe") and DeviceName !in~ ("jump01","vulnscan01")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the source host and initiating process; distinguish sanctioned scanners/automation (known service accounts, expected schedule) from an unexpected process driving the fan-out. Check whether port 5555 (ADB) is in the mix — that is not normal enterprise traffic. 2) CONTAIN: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, block outbound 22/23/5555 from it, and treat as RustDuck-infected. 3) HUNT: correlate the same host against the loader-hash and C2 UCs, and enumerate which external targets accepted the connection to gauge downstream spread.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess" or ActionType == "ConnectionAttempt"
| where RemotePort in (22, 23, 5555)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), SampleTargets = make_set(RemoteIP, 20), Ports = make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctTargets > 50
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort in (22, 23, 5555)
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), SampleTargets = make_set(DestinationIP, 20), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctTargets > 50
| order by DistinctTargets desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:(22 OR 23 OR 5555)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| in(RemotePort, values=[22,23,5555])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true), field=distinct_targets)
| distinct_targets > 50
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action
| filter dstPort in [22, 23, 5555] and action = "ACCEPT"
| stats count_distinct(dstAddr) as distinctTargets by srcAddr
| filter distinctTargets > 50
| sort distinctTargets desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_targets count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (22,23,5555) All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.src _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")`
| where distinct_targets > 50
| sort - distinct_targets
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_targets count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (22,23,5555) All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.src _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")`
| where distinct_targets > 50
| sort - distinct_targets

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser

    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |

    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",

        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1204.002

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
