Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

Langflow Python endpoint spawning shell to fetch payload via curl/wget (CVE-2026-33017 RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-33017 exploitation chain where an unauthenticated Langflow API endpoint evaluates attacker Python that forks a shell running curl/wget to pull the lambsys dropper. Article-specific because it pins the Langflow/uvicorn/python parent spawning sh -c with a remote-fetch utility. Rationale: Chains the article's explicit description: an unauthenticated Langflow endpoint evaluates Python that 'launches a remotely hosted shell script' fetched with curl or wget. Parent(python/uvicorn)+child(sh)+curl/wget is high-fidelity for this RCE-to-dropper step.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow/Python apps legitimately invoking curl/wget in a subprocess for model or dataset downloads
  • CI/CD deployment scripts run under a gunicorn-managed venv that fetch dependencies
  • Custom Langflow flows that shell out to curl for HTTP integration testing
  • Container entrypoint scripts pulling assets on first boot
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("pip install","requirements.txt","apt-get","model_download")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child cmdline and the fetched URL/IP; confirm the parent Langflow process is internet-exposed and whether the API request that triggered it was unauthenticated. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the python/langflow worker and any lambsys child, block egress to the fetched host at the firewall. 3) Hunt: search the same host for lambsys execution, cron edits under /var/spool/cron, and beacons to 83.142.209.214 / 94.156.64.241; verify Langflow is patched for CVE-2026-33017.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","langflow","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Facility in ("authpriv","user","daemon")
| where ProcessName in~ ("python","python3","langflow","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("sh -c","bash -c")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("curl","wget")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

lambsys ELF dropper/miner execution and detached launch AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution of the Go ELF binary 'lambsys' (the campaign's dropper/miner loader) by filename, path, or reference in a shell command line, including its detached launch (nohup/setsid/&). Article-specific because 'lambsys' is the named custom binary. Rationale: 'lambsys' is the article's explicitly named custom Go ELF binary that checks if it is already running, launches detached, and loads XMRig. Filename + provided SHA256/MD5 hashes make this an alerting-grade, campaign-specific detection.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1543 T1496
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Extremely unlikely benign hit — 'lambsys' is not a standard package name
  • A security tool or sandbox re-running the sample for analysis
  • Backup/AV quarantine paths that retain the binary name in a scan log
  • An internal IR playbook file or note containing the string 'lambsys'
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary hash against the three campaign SHA256s and note the executing user/path and parent process. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the lambsys process tree, capture the binary for forensics before it self-wipes the extracted XMRig TAR. 3) Hunt: enumerate SSH-reachable hosts from ~/.ssh/known_hosts and authorized_keys for lateral spread, and check for the miner TAR fetch and beacon to 83.142.209.214.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "lambsys" or ProcessCommandLine has "lambsys" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "lambsys"
| where SHA256 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc","33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df","ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2") or ProcessCommandLine has "lambsys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "lambsys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="lambsys" OR Processes.process="*lambsys*" OR Processes.process="*setsid*lambsys*" OR Processes.process="*nohup*lambsys*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Cryptojacker security-control teardown: mass pkill of rival miners + firewall/LSM disable AIInstallation High
Hunts the lambsys defense-evasion cascade: dozens of sh -c subprocesses running pkill against Kinsing/WatchDog/Rocke/Outlaw and disabling AppArmor, ufw, iptables, SELinux, the NMI watchdog and the Aliyun agent. Article-specific via the named rival families and the exact controls disabled. Rationale: Uses the article's named rival families (Kinsing, WatchDog, Rocke, Outlaw) and the exact controls lambsys disables (AppArmor, ufw, iptables, SELinux, NMI watchdog, Aliyun agent). The >5 threshold reflects the described cascade of ~51 short-lived pkill/chattr/sysctl subprocesses.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1562.004 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin hardening or firewall-migration scripts that stop ufw/iptables during a maintenance window
  • Config-management runs (Ansible/Chef) that toggle SELinux/AppArmor across a fleet
  • Alibaba Cloud agent uninstall during a legitimate cloud migration
  • AV/EDR product removing a genuine Kinsing infection (would show its own vendor binary as parent)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","chef-client","puppet","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the full set of child commands under the single parent PID — a single process firing pkill + setenforce + ufw disable + aliyun-kill in seconds is not admin activity. 2) Contain: isolate host, re-enable AppArmor/SELinux/ufw, kill the parent process tree. 3) Hunt: look for the lambsys binary, cron persistence, and the miner beacon on the same host; check whether host security agents were tampered with.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("pkill","systemctl","service","setenforce","ufw","aa-teardown","sysctl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("kinsing","kdevtmpfsi","watchdog","apparmor","ufw disable","iptables","setenforce 0","nmi_watchdog","aliyun","AliYunDun","selinux")
| summarize CmdCount = count(), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 60), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName
| where CmdCount > 5   // lambsys forks ~51 short-lived pkill/chattr/sysctl children per run
| order by LastSeen desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("pkill","setenforce 0","ufw disable","systemctl stop apparmor","iptables -F","nmi_watchdog","aliyun","AliYunDun")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("kinsing","kdevtmpfsi","watchdog","apparmor","iptables","selinux","aliyun")
| summarize CmdCount = count(), Cmds = make_set(SyslogMessage, 60) by Computer, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where CmdCount > 5
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:pkill OR @process.name:setenforce OR @process.name:ufw OR @process.name:systemctl OR @process.name:sysctl) (@process.command_line:*kinsing* OR @process.command_line:*kdevtmpfsi* OR @process.command_line:*apparmor* OR @process.command_line:*"ufw disable"* OR @process.command_line:*"setenforce 0"* OR @process.command_line:*nmi_watchdog* OR @process.command_line:*aliyun* OR @process.command_line:*AliYunDun*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(pkill|setenforce|ufw|systemctl|sysctl|service)$/i | regex("(kinsing|kdevtmpfsi|watchdog|apparmor|ufw disable|setenforce 0|iptables|nmi_watchdog|aliyun|AliYunDun|selinux)", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count()) | count > 5
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as cmds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("pkill","systemctl","service","setenforce","ufw","aa-teardown","sysctl")) AND (Processes.process="*kinsing*" OR Processes.process="*watchdog*" OR Processes.process="*kdevtmpfsi*" OR Processes.process="*apparmor*" OR Processes.process="*ufw disable*" OR Processes.process="*iptables*" OR Processes.process="*setenforce 0*" OR Processes.process="*nmi_watchdog*" OR Processes.process="*aliyun*" OR Processes.process="*AliYunDun*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count > 5 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("pkill","systemctl","service","setenforce","ufw","aa-teardown","sysctl")) AND (Processes.process="*kinsing*" OR Processes.process="*watchdog*" OR Processes.process="*kdevtmpfsi*" OR Processes.process="*apparmor*" OR Processes.process="*ufw disable*" OR Processes.process="*iptables*" OR Processes.process="*setenforce 0*" OR Processes.process="*nmi_watchdog*" OR Processes.process="*aliyun*" OR Processes.process="*AliYunDun*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count > 5 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
lambsys immutable-flag manipulation on cron/ld.so.preload/SSH persistence paths AIInstallation High
Detects the chattr -i / chattr +i sequence lambsys uses to unlock and re-lock persistence-critical files (~/.ssh, authorized_keys, /etc/crontab, /etc/ld.so.preload, /tmp, /var/tmp, /var/spool/cron). Article-specific via the exact file set and the +i re-lock of /tmp and /var/tmp. Rationale: The article lists the precise files lambsys unlocks/relocks with chattr (~/.ssh, authorized_keys, /etc/crontab, /etc/ld.so.preload, /tmp, /var/tmp, /var/spool/cron) and notes it re-applies +i to /tmp and /var/tmp — a rare, high-fidelity persistence-hardening behaviour.
ATT&CKT1222.002 T1546.008 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hardening frameworks (CIS benchmark scripts) that set +i on /etc/crontab or ld.so.preload
  • A sysadmin protecting authorized_keys with chattr +i as a deliberate control
  • Backup tooling temporarily clearing immutable flags to restore files
  • Another cryptominer family using the same chattr technique (still malicious — triage accordingly)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("cis-","hardening","ansible","restore")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the chattr target list and the parent process; a single process chattr-ing ld.so.preload + cron + .ssh in sequence is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate host; run `lsattr` on the listed paths, remove attacker +i flags, inspect /etc/ld.so.preload and /var/spool/cron for injected entries, rotate exposed SSH keys. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent (lambsys/shell) and enumerate SSH-reachable hosts for lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "chattr"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ld.so.preload","/var/spool/cron","/etc/crontab","authorized_keys",".ssh","/tmp","/var/tmp")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("+i","-i")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "chattr"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("ld.so.preload","/var/spool/cron","/etc/crontab","authorized_keys",".ssh")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("+i","-i")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

lambsys C2 beacon to 83.142.209.214 / 94.156.64.241 and ipinfo.io geolocation lookup AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections to the campaign C2 (83.142.209.214:80, 94.156.64.241) used to fetch the shell script, miner binary and XMRig TAR, plus the ipinfo.io lookup lambsys performs for pool-selection/geo-fencing. Article-specific via the hardcoded C2 IPs and ipinfo.io usage. Rationale: 83.142.209.214:80 is the article's explicit beacon/download server and 94.156.64.241 is a pre-extracted campaign IP; ipinfo.io is the named geolocation service used for pool selection and geo-fencing. Hardcoded IOCs make this alerting-grade.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1614
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate apps calling ipinfo.io for geolocation (common in analytics SDKs) — the IP hits are the strong signal, ipinfo.io alone is weaker
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling deliberately resolving the C2 IPs in a sandbox
  • Security scanners connecting to the IPs for confirmation
  • Shared-hosting reuse if the C2 IP is later reassigned (validate timestamp against the Mar27–Apr15 2026 window)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process for the C2 IP connections — if it is lambsys/curl/wget under a Langflow host, treat as confirmed. 2) Contain: block 83.142.209.214 and 94.156.64.241 at the egress firewall, isolate the host, kill the beaconing process. 3) Hunt: sweep all internet-facing Langflow hosts for connections to these IPs and to mining-pool infrastructure; confirm CVE-2026-33017 patch status.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("83.142.209.214","94.156.64.241") or RemoteUrl has "ipinfo.io"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("83.142.209.214","94.156.64.241") or DestinationHostName has "ipinfo.io" or RequestURL has "ipinfo.io"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XMRig Monero miner execution and mining-pool Stratum egress on Langflow hosts AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the final-stage bespoke XMRig miner: execution by name/args (--donate-level, stratum+tcp, cryptonight, -o pool) and outbound Stratum connections on common pool ports (3333/5555/7777/9999/14444). Scopes to server/Langflow hosts to catch the resource-hijacking impact. Article-specific via the named XMRig payload delivered by lambsys. Rationale: The article states lambsys extracts and runs a bespoke XMRig miner as its final stage. XMRig binary name and its distinctive Stratum/RandomX/--donate-level arguments are the highest-fidelity, deployment-agnostic indicators of the Monero-mining impact described.
ATT&CKT1496 T1071
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned in-house mining / benchmarking on a dev box (rare on a Langflow app server)
  • Security research reproducing XMRig in a lab
  • A monitoring agent whose config string legitimately contains 'randomx' or 'cryptonight' (unlikely)
  • Password-cracking or crypto-benchmark tools sharing RandomX libraries
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName in (SecurityServerList) == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain leads back to lambsys/Langflow and extract the -o pool address and wallet from the command line. 2) Contain: kill the xmrig process, isolate the host, block the mining-pool destination, and preserve the binary before it self-wipes. 3) Hunt: correlate with the C2 IPs and cron persistence on the same host, and check all Langflow endpoints for CVE-2026-33017 exploitation and reused-SSH-key lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "xmrig"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("stratum+tcp","--donate-level","cryptonight","--coin monero","randomx","--cpu-priority")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("xmrig","stratum+tcp","--donate-level","cryptonight","randomx","--coin monero")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access

    category: file_access

detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'

falsepositives:

    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8") or SHA1 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8") or MD5 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8") or SHA1 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8") or MD5 in~ ("71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["71af8bd9b8019b7e5f460ce4c5c14ff7716a2c2faaaf1f274ceaa54cb89723bc", "33588aa446984d3340cab686d38f2aa85a70eb3f76c459da3eef0304592b99df", "ddde47bf00324075c7eeb0b9d0ff0a5d1b95bfc619aca4b5def85263838212f2", "46096a72d84db5f1dafd944fcf6571c8"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-browser process writing Chromium 'Secure Preferences'/'Preferences' (Silent Swap sideload) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Silent Swap covert extension install: a non-browser process (the unsigned .NET BaseZipInstaller or Golang variant) writing to a Chromium 'Secure Preferences' or 'Preferences' file under a browser User Data profile. Normally only the browser itself writes these HMAC-protected files; a third-party writer indicates the malware tampering with protected settings to silently register the fake 'Google Notes' extension. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit covert-install mechanic: the malware modifies the browser's HMAC-protected 'Secure Preferences'/'Preferences' files (under User Data) from a non-browser installer. Limiting the writer to non-browser processes makes this very high-fidelity since legit modification is browser-exclusive. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/silent-swap-crypto-clipper-uses-fake.html • https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~andrei/cans20.pdf
ATT&CKT1176.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browser profile migration/sync tools (e.g. third-party bookmark importers) writing Preferences
  • Enterprise browser management/GPO agents pushing managed extension policy
  • Antivirus or backup software touching the User Data folder and re-writing Preferences
  • Browser repair/reset utilities run by IT support
  • Roaming-profile redirection writing Preferences on logon
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","vivaldi.exe","opera.exe","opera_gx.exe","update.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe","googleupdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe") or InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 and FolderPath; check if the writer is signed and known. Pull the modified 'Secure Preferences' and diff the 'extensions.settings' / 'extensions.ui.developer_mode' nodes for an unfamiliar extension ID claiming 'Google Notes'. 2) Contain: kill the installer process, isolate the host, and remove the rogue extension from every Chromium profile; reset Secure Preferences. Treat any crypto wallet addresses copied during the window as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writer's SHA256 across the fleet, check for self-deleted installers and ZIP retrievals, and look for the C2 connections in UC3.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("Secure Preferences","Preferences")
| where FolderPath has @"\User Data\"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\", @"\Vivaldi\", @"\Opera Software\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","vivaldi.exe","opera.exe","opera_gx.exe","update.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe","googleupdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe","msedge_proxy.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Secure Preferences","Preferences")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\User Data\"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\", @"\Vivaldi\", @"\Opera Software\")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","vivaldi.exe","opera.exe","opera_gx.exe","update.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe","googleupdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe"))
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Browser Process Modifying Chromium Secure Preferences (Silent Swap Extension Sideload)
id: 7b3e9c2a-1d4f-4a8b-9c6e-2f5a8d1b4c30
status: experimental
description: Detects a non-browser process writing to a Chromium 'Secure Preferences' or 'Preferences' file, the covert extension-injection + HMAC-recalculation technique used by the Silent Swap crypto clipper to register a fake Google Notes extension.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/silent-swap-crypto-clipper-uses-fake.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1176.001
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\User Data\'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\Secure Preferences'
      - '\Preferences'
  filter_browser:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\vivaldi.exe'
      - '\opera.exe'
      - '\update.exe'
      - '\software_reporter_tool.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
  - Browser sync or profile-migration utilities
  - Enterprise browser management agents
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\User?Data\\*Secure?Preferences OR *\\User?Data\\*Preferences) -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\vivaldi.exe OR *\\opera.exe OR *\\update.exe OR *\\Update.exe OR *\\software_reporter_tool.exe OR *\\googleupdate.exe OR *\\GoogleUpdate.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\User Data\\.*(Secure Preferences|Preferences)$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave|vivaldi|opera|opera_gx|update|software_reporter_tool|googleupdate|elevation_service|setup|msiexec)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count(as=writes))
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="Secure Preferences" OR Filesystem.file_name="Preferences") Filesystem.file_path="*\\User Data\\*" NOT (Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","vivaldi.exe","opera.exe","opera_gx.exe","update.exe","software_reporter_tool.exe","googleupdate.exe","elevation_service.exe","setup.exe","msiexec.exe")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Single process force-terminating multiple Chromium browsers (Silent Swap profile-unlock precursor) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Silent Swap pre-injection step where the installer enumerates installed Chromium browsers and forcibly terminates each one to unlock the profile files before tampering. Flags a single non-browser initiator running taskkill against two or more distinct Chromium browser binaries within a short window. Rationale: Built on the article's stated behaviour that the installer 'forcibly terminates the browser process' for each detected Chromium profile before modifying its files. Requiring >=2 distinct browser targets from one initiator separates this from a normal single-browser restart. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/silent-swap-crypto-clipper-uses-fake.html
ATT&CKT1176.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT scripts that close all browsers before a software update or imaging
  • Browser updater/installer killing the running instance before applying an update
  • User-run cleanup batch files that taskkill multiple browsers
  • Endpoint management tools (SCCM/Intune) terminating browsers for forced updates
  • RMM agents closing browsers prior to maintenance
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("update.exe","setup.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe","ccmexec.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the initiating process and parent of taskkill; legit cases trace to known updaters/RMM. Confirm whether a 'Secure Preferences' write (UC1) followed on the same host within minutes. 2) Contain: if the killer is an unknown/unsigned binary, isolate the host and capture the binary before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiator hash, search for ZIP downloads and self-deletion (file delete of own image), and check UC3 C2 connections for that host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "taskkill.exe"
| extend BrowserKilled = tolower(extract(@"(?i)(chrome|msedge|brave|vivaldi|opera|opera_gx)\.exe", 1, ProcessCommandLine))
| where isnotempty(BrowserKilled)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize KilledBrowsers = make_set(BrowserKilled), KillCount = dcount(BrowserKilled), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 8) by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where KillCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\taskkill.exe"
| extend BrowserKilled = tolower(extract(@"(?i)(chrome|msedge|brave|vivaldi|opera|opera_gx)\.exe", 1, CommandLine))
| where isnotempty(BrowserKilled)
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| summarize KilledBrowsers = make_set(BrowserKilled), KillCount = dcount(BrowserKilled), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleCmds = make_set(CommandLine, 8) by Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where KillCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\taskkill.exe OR *\\TASKKILL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*chrome.exe* OR *msedge.exe* OR *brave.exe* OR *vivaldi.exe* OR *opera.exe*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\taskkill\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(?<Browser>chrome|msedge|brave|vivaldi|opera)\.exe", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName], function=[count(field=Browser, distinct=true, as=DistinctBrowsers), collect([Browser])])
| DistinctBrowsers >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as process_cmds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="taskkill.exe" (Processes.process="*chrome.exe*" OR Processes.process="*msedge.exe*" OR Processes.process="*brave.exe*" OR Processes.process="*vivaldi.exe*" OR Processes.process="*opera.exe*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| rex max_match=0 field=process_cmds "(?i)(?<browsers>chrome|msedge|brave|vivaldi|opera)\.exe"
| eval distinct_browsers=mvcount(mvdedup(browsers))
| where distinct_browsers>=2

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| rex max_match=0 field=process_cmds "(?i)(?<browsers>chrome|msedge|brave|vivaldi|opera)\.exe"

| where distinct_browsers>=2

Silent Swap / VPN Go clipper C2 and clipboard-exfil to known infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on host connections to the confirmed Silent Swap and 'VPN Go' clipboard-stealer infrastructure: the two exfiltration IPs (178.236.252.133, 77.91.123.187) and the Silent Swap C2/dead-drop domain set. The campaign uses EtherHiding (blockchain dead-drop resolver) to rotate live C2, so these named IOCs are the durable network pivot for backend wallet-substitution and clipboard exfil. Rationale: Uses the two exfil IPs stated in the article body (Socket's VPN Go finding) and the McAfee Silent Swap C2 domain set. EtherHiding rotates the live C2, so direct-IP plus the static domain list is the most durable network pivot; 'bucket-aws-s*' domains are attacker C2, not real AWS, so no CloudWatch query applies. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/silent-swap-crypto-clipper-uses-fake.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc5142-etherhiding-distribute-malware
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.001 T1657
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An exfil IP later reassigned to shared/CDN hosting serving benign traffic
  • Security tooling or sandbox detonating a sample and contacting the IOC IP
  • Threat-intel/research workstations intentionally resolving the C2 domains
  • A look-alike domain typo coincidentally matching a benign service
  • Proxy/egress appliance pre-fetching URLs for inspection
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","sense.exe","wireshark.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection and whether it is a browser (extension-driven exfil) or the installer. Confirm the host also shows UC1/UC2 activity. 2) Contain: block the IPs/domains at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and remove the rogue extension; rotate any secrets/seed phrases and warn the user that copied wallet addresses may have been swapped. 3) Hunt: sweep DNS/proxy logs org-wide for the full domain list, pivot on the connecting process hash, and check for blockchain RPC traffic indicative of EtherHiding dead-drop resolution.
let c2_ips = dynamic(["178.236.252.133","77.91.123.187"]);
let c2_domains = dynamic(["hell1-kitty.cc","alphazero1-endscape.cc","api-microservice-us1.com","bucket-aws-s1.com","bucket-aws-s2.com","fileless-storage-s3.cc","globalsnn1-new.cc","globalsnn2-new.cc","globalsnn3-new.cc","handle-me-sv1.com","hardware-office.cc","health-smooth-eu1.com","health-smooth-eu2.com","health-smooth-eu3.com","holiday-updateservice.com","memory-protection-layer1.cc","memory-protection-layer2.cc","microservice-update-s1-bucket.cc","microservice-update-s2-bucket.cc","my-smart-house1.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (c2_ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (c2_domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2_ips = dynamic(["178.236.252.133","77.91.123.187"]);
let c2_domains = dynamic(["hell1-kitty.cc","alphazero1-endscape.cc","api-microservice-us1.com","bucket-aws-s1.com","bucket-aws-s2.com","fileless-storage-s3.cc","globalsnn1-new.cc","globalsnn2-new.cc","globalsnn3-new.cc","handle-me-sv1.com","hardware-office.cc","health-smooth-eu1.com","health-smooth-eu2.com","health-smooth-eu3.com","holiday-updateservice.com","memory-protection-layer1.cc","memory-protection-layer2.cc","microservice-update-s1-bucket.cc","microservice-update-s2-bucket.cc","my-smart-house1.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr in (c2_ips)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Dst=DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, Signal="NetworkToC2IP" ),
( ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (c2_domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Dst=DnsQuery, DstPortNumber=int(null), Url="", Signal="DnsToC2Domain" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: critical

GuardFall Exposes Open-Source AI Coding Agents to Decades-Old Shell Injection Risks

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 10 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The safety check that is supposed to stop an AI coding agent from running a dangerous command can be walked straight past using a shell trick that has been public for decades. New research from&nbsp;Adversa AI, which is named the bypass GuardFall, found it works against ten of the eleven popular open-source coding and computer-use agents the firm tested. Only one, "Continue," was built to

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Untrusted in-repo AI agent config (.aider.conf.yml) landing from clone/checkout · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Shell blocklist bypass via empty-quote/token-split binary names (GuardFall) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Open-source AI coding agent auto-execute flag spawning a shell · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AI agent shell reaching into ~/.ssh / ~/.aws credential files · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Shell blocklist bypass via empty-quote/token-split binary names (GuardFall) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts AI-coding-agent-spawned shells running commands obfuscated to defeat plain-text blocklists: empty-quote/backslash-split binary names (r''m), base64 piped into sh/bash, or benign tools (find/dd) given destructive flags. This is the exact GuardFall evasion shape where bash rewrites the string after the agent's filter inspected it. Rationale: Uses the article's literal GuardFall evasion primitives (empty-quote split like r''m, base64-pipe-to-shell, destructive find/dd flags) anchored to the named open-source agent binaries as parents — the combination of agent-parent + shell-child + obfuscated cmdline is far higher-fidelity than any single clause. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22040
ATT&CKT1027.010 T1140 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately running a build script that base64-decodes an embedded asset and pipes it to a shell installer
  • CI/dev tooling using find -delete to clean build artifacts
  • dd used for legitimate disk imaging by a sysadmin on a dev box
  • Shell aliases or generated scripts that happen to contain quote-adjacent tokens
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run build","make ","cmake","docker build") and ProcessCommandLine has "-delete")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode any base64; confirm the parent is an AI coding agent and whether the session was non-interactive/auto-exec. Identify the repo/working dir the agent was pointed at. 2) Contain: kill the agent + shell processes, revoke and rotate any credentials reachable from $HOME (~/.ssh, ~/.aws), and quarantine the host from prod networks. 3) Hunt: review the triggering repo/PR (especially fork PRs and in-repo config like .aider.conf.yml) for the injected instruction; sweep other dev hosts for the same agent-parent + obfuscated-shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)([a-z])'{2,}[a-z]|base64\s+-d.*\|\s*(ba)?sh|\bdd\s+.+of=/dev/|find\s+.+-delete|find\s+.+-exec\s+rm"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Open-source AI coding agent auto-execute flag spawning a shell AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the GuardFall precondition: a named open-source coding agent invoked with an auto-execute / skip-permissions flag (--auto-exec, --auto-run, --auto-test, --yes-always, dangerously-skip-permissions) that then spawns a shell or interpreter non-interactively. This is the unattended configuration that lets an injected command actually run. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit auto-execute flag names (--auto-exec/--auto-run/--auto-test/dangerously-skip-permissions) AND the named agent binaries spawning a shell — the unattended-execution precondition the article says must be true for the attack to land, making it a high-fidelity governance/posture alert. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://www.theregister.com/2026/04/01/claude_code_rule_cap_raises/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal CI pipeline that intentionally runs an agent unattended on trusted internal repos
  • Developer using --yes-always on their own local repo for a known refactor
  • Automated test harness invoking the agent with --auto-test against a sandboxed branch
  • Demo/eval scripts running an agent non-interactively in a throwaway container
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("ci-runner","build-agent") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--auto-test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the agent run was sanctioned (internal trusted repo vs fork/external) and which repo/working dir it targeted; capture the child shell command lines. 2) Contain: if the repo source is untrusted or unknown, terminate the agent session and disable the auto-execute flag in the relevant wrapper/CI job; isolate the host pending review. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts/CI runners running these agents with auto-exec flags, and correlate forward to credential-file reads or outbound connections from the spawned shells.

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

AI agent shell reaching into ~/.ssh / ~/.aws credential files AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GuardFall credential-theft payload: a shell or copy/transfer tool spawned by an AI coding agent that reads SSH keys, cloud credentials, or other home-folder secrets. Targets the article's stated impact — stealing 'SSH keys and cloud credentials to anything sitting in your home folder'. Rationale: Combines the article's named agent binaries as parent with the exact credential paths it calls out (SSH keys, AWS/cloud creds in $HOME) referenced by a read/copy/transfer child process — agent-spawned access to ~/.ssh or ~/.aws is well outside normal agent working-dir behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/ • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.22040
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An agent legitimately tasked with configuring git over SSH or deploying via scp reading ~/.ssh/config
  • Developer-driven 'aws configure' or terraform run that the agent shells out to and which touches ~/.aws/credentials
  • Backup or dotfile-sync tooling invoked through the agent's shell
  • Agent reading ~/.docker/config.json to run an authorized image build
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws configure","git@","ssh -T","terraform") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the credential access matched the task the user gave the agent; capture the destination of any subsequent cp/scp/curl. 2) Contain: immediately rotate the specific keys/credentials touched (SSH keypairs, AWS access keys, kube tokens) and revoke sessions; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents/NetworkConnectIP4 from the same shell for outbound exfil shortly after the read, and review the source repo/PR that the agent was operating on.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cat","cp","tar","scp","curl","wget","base64")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.ssh/id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\.aws/credentials|\.config/gcloud|\.kube/config|\.netrc|\.docker/config\.json"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("aider","goose","cline","plandex","opencode","open-interpreter","openhands","swe-agent","node","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cat","cp","tar","scp","curl","wget","base64")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.ssh/id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\.aws/credentials|\.config/gcloud|\.kube/config|\.netrc|\.docker/config\.json"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
