Untrusted in-repo AI agent config (.aider.conf.yml) landing from clone/checkout AIDelivery Low
Hunts the GuardFall initial-access vector where a malicious agent config file shipped inside a repository (the article calls out .aider.conf.yml) is written to disk by a VCS/clone or the agent itself, which can trigger the attack on the first accepted edit. Treats in-repo agent config as untrusted code. Rationale: Uses the exact config filename the article names as untrusted-code (.aider.conf.yml) written by a clone/checkout or the agent — a focused hunting pivot for the supply-chain delivery step, kept low-confidence/hunting because legitimate repos also ship this file. Cross-checked against: • https://adversa.ai/blog/the-approval-prompt-is-lying-to-you-symlink-rce-in-five-ai-coding-agents-claude-code-cursor-antigravity-copilot-grok-build/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately commits .aider.conf.yml to share project agent settings
  • Developer cloning their own trusted repo that contains the config
  • Templating/scaffolding tools generating an aider config
  • CI checkout of an internal repo that ships the file by policy
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/internal-repos/","/trusted/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the contents of the written .aider.conf.yml for embedded auto-run/auto-commit settings, shell hooks, or instructions, and identify the source repo/PR (especially fork PRs). 2) Contain: if the repo is untrusted/external, prevent the agent from running against it, move $HOME to a throwaway folder per the article's guidance, and disable auto-execute. 3) Hunt: correlate forward to agent-spawned shells (UC1/UC2) and credential reads (UC3) on the same host within the session window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ (".aider.conf.yml",".aider.conf.yaml","aider.conf.yml")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","node","python","python3","aider","tar","unzip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ (".aider.conf.yml",".aider.conf.yaml","aider.conf.yml")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("git","node","python","python3","aider","tar","unzip")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

What the Numbers Say About FIFA 2026 Cyber Risk

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 11 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The FIFA World Cup 2026 opened on June 11. By that date, according to Check Point Research, the fraud infrastructure targeting it had already been built, staged, and partially deployed. Threat actor activity was pre-planned, months out, across three sectors and at least ten languages. Check Point Exposure Management published the FIFA World Cup 2026 Cyber Threat Report this month, covering

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Network/DNS contact with FIFA World Cup 2026 lookalike fraud domains · [LLM] Inbound mail or embedded URL from FIFA 2026 impersonation domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Network/DNS contact with FIFA World Cup 2026 lookalike fraud domains AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS resolutions and network connections to the specific FIFA 2026 brand-impersonation domains staged by the Check Point / Group-IB-tracked fraud infrastructure (hospitality, store, and gambling lures). Article-specific because it pins the named registered domains rather than a generic 'newly-registered domain' heuristic. Rationale: Uses the seven concrete lookalike domains from the article's IOC bundle (www-fifa.me/.co, 26-fifa.com, op.shop-26fifa.com, fifaofficialstore.shop, fifa2026guess.com, fortune-worldcup2026.com.cn); these are dedicated fraud-only domains so any resolution is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against the FBI IC3 PSA and Check Point's research blog which independently confirm the campaign and several of the same domains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260527 • https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/before-the-first-whistle-how-cyber-criminals-are-targeting-world-cup-2026/ • https://www.gblock.app/articles/fifa-2026-phishing-wave-fake-domains-email-scams
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or threat-intel platform manually browsing the domain during triage
  • Automated URL-detonation sandbox / SOAR enrichment visiting the domain from a known scanning host
  • Secure web gateway pre-fetch or link-rewrite service resolving the URL on the user's behalf
  • Brand-protection / takedown vendor crawling the domain from corporate ranges
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-sandbox","svc-urlscan") and DeviceName !in~ ("SOC-SANDBOX01","PROXY-SCAN01")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the host/user and the initiating process from DeviceNetworkEvents — confirm it was a browser/mail client (real user) vs a sandbox/proxy host, and whether a file download or credential-entry POST followed within 5 min. 2) CONTAIN: sinkhole/block the domain at DNS and the secure web gateway tenant-wide; if the user submitted data, force a password reset + revoke sessions and isolate the host if a payload landed. 3) HUNT: pivot on the resolved IP and registrar pattern (.top, GoDaddy/Hostinger/Namecheap/Porkbun/IONOS) to surface sibling FIFA lookalikes the same host or org touched; review EmailEvents for the delivering message.

Inbound mail or embedded URL from FIFA 2026 impersonation domains AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound email whose sender domain (envelope or header-from) or embedded URL belongs to the FIFA World Cup 2026 fraud domains — the article notes a subset have MX records configured for reply-path impersonation and password-reset interception. Article-specific via the named domains rather than a generic spoofing rule. Rationale: Anchors on the same seven named fraud domains but on the mail vector (SenderFromDomain / SenderMailFromDomain / embedded URL), targeting the reply-path-impersonation and password-reset-interception use the article calls out for the MX-enabled subset. Domains corroborated by FBI IC3 and Check Point; mail tracing is uniquely a Defender-for-O365 signal, so other platforms are left blank. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260527 • https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/before-the-first-whistle-how-cyber-criminals-are-targeting-world-cup-2026/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal phishing-simulation platform using a FIFA-themed lure domain that overlaps a string
  • Brand-protection vendor sending sample/takedown-notice mail referencing the domains
  • Threat-intel newsletter or this very article being forwarded internally with the domains in the body (URL match on a benign report)
  • Quarantined/blocked messages surfacing in the hunt even though they never reached a user (DeliveryAction = Blocked/Quarantine)
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryLocation in ("Inbox","JunkFolder") and SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourphishsimvendor.com"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation — prioritize messages Delivered to Inbox; check whether the recipient clicked (UrlClickEvents) or replied. 2) CONTAIN: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide via Explorer, block the sender domain and embedded URL, and if any recipient entered credentials or replied to a reply-path lure, force password reset + revoke tokens. 3) HUNT: search for the same sender infrastructure (shared IP/SPF record) hitting other mailboxes and correlate recipients against the UC1 network/DNS hits to find users who both received and visited the domain.

let urlMsgs = EmailUrlInfo

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Attackers Exploit SimpleHelp CVE-2026-48558 to Deploy TaskWeaver and Djinn Stealer

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An unknown threat actor has been observed exploiting a recently disclosed maximum-severity security flaw in SimpleHelp to deliver two previously unreported malware families, TaskWeaver and Djinn Stealer. The intrusion involves the exploitation of CVE-2026-48558 (CVSS score: 10.0), a critical authentication bypass vulnerability impacting the OpenID Connect (OIDC) flow that an unauthenticated

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SimpleHelp RMM service spawning node.exe/script interpreter (CVE-2026-48558 post-exploit) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Attackers Exploit SimpleHelp CVE-2026-48558 to Deploy TaskWeaver and Djinn Steal

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Djinn Stealer credential-store harvesting by node.exe (cloud/SSH/AI-assistant configs) · [LLM] Djinn Stealer exfiltration to 96.126.130.126:58942 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
SimpleHelp RMM service spawning node.exe/script interpreter (CVE-2026-48558 post-exploit) AIExploitation High
Hunts the SimpleHelp remote-access service launching node.exe or a script host, the post-auth command-execution step after CVE-2026-48558 forged-OIDC technician takeover. SimpleHelp's endpoint service legitimately runs Java helper code, never Node.js or shells, so this parent-child pair is the exploitation fingerprint. Rationale: Pairs the article's exploited product (SimpleHelp RMM, CVE-2026-48558) with its confirmed endpoint service binaries/paths (SimpleService.exe, Manage Remote Access Service.exe, JWrapper-Remote Access) as parent of node.exe — the documented TaskWeaver delivery runtime. Parent+child both pinned makes it high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-critical-simplehelp-flaw-deploy-new-djinn-infostealer-taskweaver-malware/ • https://github.com/anvilogic-forge/armory/blob/main/detections/endpoint/simplehelp_remote_access_tool_execution/simplehelp_remote_access_tool_execution-splunk-edr.yml • https://www.file.net/process/simpleservice.exe.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MSP technician running ad-hoc PowerShell/cmd scripts on managed endpoints via SimpleHelp
  • Approved software-deployment scripts pushed through the RMM toolbox
  • IT automation that legitimately bundles a Node.js helper executed by node.exe
  • Patch/inventory routines spawning wscript/cscript from the RMM agent
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("Get-Inventory","\\RMM\\scripts\\") and AccountName in~ ("svc-rmm","msp-automation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child command line and SHA256; confirm whether node.exe is executing a file named jquery.js (UC2) and whether the technician session that drove it maps to a known MSP staff login or a forged/self-registered OIDC technician on the SimpleHelp server. 2) Contain: isolate the host, suspend the SimpleHelp server's OIDC auth (or block the server externally) and revoke/disable the rogue technician account; confirm CVE-2026-48558 patch level. 3) Hunt: sweep all RMM-managed endpoints for node.exe+jquery.js, connections to dev-tunnels.com, and 96.126.130.126:58942.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("SimpleService.exe","Manage Remote Access Service.exe","Remote Access.exe")) or (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\JWrapper-Remote Access\", @"\JWrapper-Remote Support\"))
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\SimpleService.exe", @"\Manage Remote Access Service.exe", @"\Remote Access.exe", @"\JWrapper-Remote Access\", @"\JWrapper-Remote Support\")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\node.exe", @"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\mshta.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SimpleHelp Remote Access Service Spawning Script Interpreter
id: 9f3b1c42-7a6e-4e21-9b2d-1c5e8a0f4d11
status: experimental
description: Detects the SimpleHelp RMM remote-access service spawning node.exe or a script interpreter, as seen in CVE-2026-48558 exploitation deploying TaskWeaver.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html
  - https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1219
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\SimpleService.exe'
      - '\Manage Remote Access Service.exe'
      - '\Remote Access.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:(*\\SimpleService.exe OR *\\simpleservice.exe OR *\\JWrapper-Remote\ Access\\* OR *\\JWrapper-Remote\ Support\\*)) (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\node.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\mshta.exe))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/(simpleservice|manage remote access service|remote access)\.exe$/i OR ParentImageFileName=/JWrapper-Remote (Access|Support)/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(node|cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("SimpleService.exe","Manage Remote Access Service.exe","Remote Access.exe") OR Processes.parent_process_path="*JWrapper-Remote Access*" OR Processes.parent_process_path="*JWrapper-Remote Support*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("node.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("SimpleService.exe","Manage Remote Access Service.exe","Remote Access.exe") OR Processes.parent_process_path="*JWrapper-Remote Access*" OR Processes.parent_process_path="*JWrapper-Remote Support*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("node.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
TaskWeaver Node.js loader: node.exe executing jquery.js AIInstallation High
Hunts node.exe executing a script named jquery.js — the exact TaskWeaver loader disguise reported by Blackpoint. jquery.js is a browser library that is never legitimately run by the Node.js interpreter, making node.exe+jquery.js a near-zero-FP signature. Rationale: Uses the article's literal TaskWeaver tradecraft — 'delivered as jquery.js and executed through node.exe'. A browser library name passed to the Node.js runtime is a contradiction in legitimate use, giving a clean single-event alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer deliberately running a Node test harness file they happened to name jquery.js
  • A frontend build/bundler step that shells out node against a vendored jquery.js (rare — usually bundlers read it, not exec it)
  • Security testing/red-team replaying this exact TTP in a lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\", @"\AppData\Roaming\npm\") and ProcessCommandLine has "--test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: collect the node.exe SHA256, full command line, the jquery.js path and its parent process; confirm whether the parent is the SimpleHelp service (UC1) or a temp/AppData drop. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node.exe tree, and quarantine the jquery.js artifact for reversing. 3) Hunt: on the same host and across managed fleet, look for the C2 callout to dev-tunnels.com (UC3), credential-store access by node.exe (UC4), and exfil to 96.126.130.126:58942 (UC5).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "jquery.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TaskWeaver Node.js Loader Executing jquery.js
id: a1d7c8e9-2b34-4c50-8f6a-7e9d0b2a3c44
status: experimental
description: Detects node.exe executing a script named jquery.js, the TaskWeaver loader disguise behind the SimpleHelp CVE-2026-48558 intrusions.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-cve-2026.html
  - https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1027
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\node.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'jquery.js'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\node.EXE) @CommandLine:*jquery.js*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/jquery\.js/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="node.exe" Processes.process="*jquery.js*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="node.exe" Processes.process="*jquery.js*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
TaskWeaver C2 beacon to typosquatted Microsoft Dev Tunnels (dev-tunnels.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts host resolution/connection to a.dev-tunnels.com, TaskWeaver's encrypted C2 channel. The legitimate Microsoft service is devtunnels.ms; the hyphenated .com form is a deliberate typosquat, so any contact with dev-tunnels.com is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the article's named C2 host a.dev-tunnels.com. External research confirms it is a typosquat of Microsoft Dev Tunnels (legit = *.devtunnels.ms), so the hyphenated .com pattern alone is malicious and won't collide with genuine Dev Tunnels traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/attack-exploiting-simplehelp-vulnerability-deploys-novel-loader-infostealer
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected for the exact dev-tunnels.com string; the legitimate service is devtunnels.ms and would not match
  • Internal threat-intel/sandbox detonation hosts deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Security researcher visiting the domain in a browser during analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the process (node.exe expected per DeviceNetworkEvents); correlate to a node.exe+jquery.js execution (UC2) in the prior minutes. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block dev-tunnels.com at DNS and egress, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: across the fleet for any dev-tunnels.com resolution and for subsequent exfil to 96.126.130.126:58942 (UC5); review which credentials the host could reach (cloud, SCM, AI tools) for forced rotation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "dev-tunnels.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "dev-tunnels.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Djinn Stealer credential-store harvesting by node.exe (cloud/SSH/AI-assistant configs) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the TaskWeaver node.exe runtime touching multiple distinct developer credential stores in one process — .aws/.azure/gcloud/.oci, .ssh, gh CLI, Docker, npmrc, AI-assistant configs (Claude/Codex/Cline/OpenCode), and crypto wallets. The breadth across cloud+SCM+AI+wallet stores in a single node.exe is the Djinn Stealer collection fingerprint. Rationale: Enumerates the exact credential-store set the article attributes to Djinn Stealer (AWS/Azure/GCP/OCI, gh CLI, Docker, npm, .ssh, AI assistants Claude/Codex/Cline/OpenCode, crypto wallets), and requires >=3 distinct stores touched by a single node.exe to separate stealer fan-out from a developer reading one config. Caveat: file-read telemetry is partial on Defender (reads not always logged); Falcon FileOpenInfo gives the cleanest read visibility, hence hunting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/djinn-stealer-targets-cloud-ai-credentials • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://devops.com/attackers-exploit-simplehelp-flaw-to-steal-info-from-ai-coding-assistants-clouds/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Node-based dev tool (e.g. an IaC CLI or AI coding agent) legitimately reading .aws + .ssh + .docker during normal work
  • CI/build agents running node that load multiple registry/cloud creds
  • Backup/sync software wrapping node touching dotfile config dirs
  • A developer's terminal AI assistant enumerating its own .config on startup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\", @"\AppData\Roaming\npm\node_modules\") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("build","ci-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the node.exe maps to TaskWeaver (jquery.js cmdline/UC2) rather than a legit Node CLI; list the exact credential paths touched and timestamps. 2) Contain: isolate the host and treat every touched credential as compromised — immediately rotate cloud keys, SSH keys, gh/PATs, npm tokens, vault tokens, and move crypto wallet funds. 3) Hunt: check the rotated credentials' cloud audit logs (CloudTrail/AzureActivity) for use from attacker IPs, and look for exfil to 96.126.130.126:58942 (UC5).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.aws\", @"\.azure\", @"\.config\gcloud\", @"\.oci\", @"\.ssh\", @"\.config\gh\", @"\.docker\", @"\.kube\", @"\.npmrc", @"\.anthropic\", @"\.config\Claude\", @"\.codex\", @"\.cline\", @"\.config\opencode\", @"\.vault-token", @"\Electrum\", @"\Exodus\", @"\Ethereum\", @"\Bitcoin\")
| summarize PathCount = dcount(FolderPath), Paths = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId
| where PathCount >= 3   // breadth across >=3 distinct credential stores = stealer fan-out, not a dev touching one config
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.aws\", @"\.azure\", @"\.config\gcloud\", @"\.oci\", @"\.ssh\", @"\.config\gh\", @"\.docker\", @"\.kube\", @"\.npmrc", @"\.anthropic\", @"\.config\Claude\", @"\.codex\", @"\.cline\", @"\.config\opencode\", @"\Electrum\", @"\Exodus\")
| summarize PathCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessId
| where PathCount >= 3   // >=3 distinct credential stores touched by one node.exe
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\node.EXE) @TargetFilename:(*\\.aws\\* OR *\\.azure\\* OR *\\.config\\gcloud\\* OR *\\.ssh\\* OR *\\.config\\gh\\* OR *\\.docker\\* OR *\\.anthropic\\* OR *\\.config\\Claude\\* OR *\\.codex\\* OR *\\.cline\\* OR *\\.npmrc OR *\\Electrum\\* OR *\\Exodus\\*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/(\\\.aws\\|\\\.azure\\|\\\.config\\gcloud|\\\.oci\\|\\\.ssh\\|\\\.config\\gh|\\\.docker\\|\\\.anthropic\\|\\\.config\\Claude|\\\.codex\\|\\\.cline\\|\\\.npmrc|Electrum|Exodus)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true), as=store_count)
| store_count >= 3

Djinn Stealer exfiltration to 96.126.130.126:58942 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts any outbound connection to the article's attacker exfil endpoint 96.126.130.126 on TCP 58942 — the destination where Djinn Stealer ships its AES-256-GCM/RSA-2048 encrypted TAR.GZ of harvested credentials. A fixed IP on a high non-standard port is a near-zero-FP exfil indicator. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exfil socket 96.126.130.126:58942 (the AES-256-GCM/RSA-2048 TAR.GZ drop). A hardcoded IP plus uncommon high port is unambiguous; matching either platform's network telemetry yields an immediate, low-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-cve-2026-48558/
ATT&CKT1048 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal sandbox/threat-intel detonation host deliberately connecting to the IOC
  • Blue-team IOC validation or firewall block-rule testing against the IP
  • Shared egress/proxy IP coincidentally NATed to this destination (verify the destination, not the source)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (node.exe expected) and the source host/user; estimate bytes_out to gauge how much was exfiltrated. 2) Contain: block 96.126.130.126 at egress/firewall, isolate the host, and capture the node.exe and any staged TAR.GZ for forensics. 3) Hunt: rotate ALL credentials the host could reach (cloud, SCM, npm/registry, SSH, vault, AI-assistant tokens) and review their downstream audit logs for attacker use, since the article warns stolen creds enable later access into prod/build/cloud tenants.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "96.126.130.126" and RemotePort == 58942
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "96.126.130.126" and DestinationPort == 58942
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-06-30 11 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An in-depth analysis of Umbrij, a new tool used by the ToddyCat APT group to compromise corporate email communications in Gmail. The attack targeted OAuth authorization tokens, allowing threat actors to gain access to Google services.

ATT&CKT1027 T1053.005 T1134.003 T1190 T1204.002 T1528 T1574.002

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) · [LLM] Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary · [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading: signed host loading malicious log.dll/GoogleServices.dll from writable path · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Masquerading scheduled task 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' launching a signed binary AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence/launch step where ToddyCat created a scheduled task named KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp to run a digitally-signed sideload host. Kaspersky never creates a task with this name, so any occurrence of the string is malicious by definition. Rationale: Anchors on the exact masquerading task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' called out in the article's Execution section; it is a fixed, unique string no legitimate product emits. Cross-checked Securelist part 2 and the ToddyCat series. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-steals-email-data-from-outlook/118044/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A SOC analyst manually re-creating the task name during IR reproduction/testing
  • An internal red-team emulating ToddyCat TTPs
  • A detection-content lab importing the IOC string into a test task
  • Documentation/scripts that reference the task name in comments being scanned by inventory tooling
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the scheduled task definition (Actions/Exec path) and the signed binary it launches; verify the signer and whether the path is a writable dir (Users\Public, Temp, vss). 2) Contain: disable/delete the task, isolate the host, and capture the launched binary + any same-folder DLL for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot on the launched binary hash and folder across the fleet; check for the BDS.exe/log.dll sideload chain and Chromium remote-debugging launches on the same host within +/- 1h.

| order by Timestamp desc

| where EventID in (4698, 4702, 4699)
| where EventData has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"

ToddyCat Umbrij DLL side-loading: signed host loading malicious log.dll/GoogleServices.dll from writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact sideload pairs ToddyCat abused to launch Umbrij: BDSubWiz.exe/bds.exe loading log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder.exe loading Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll, and GoogleDesktop.exe loading GoogleServices.dll, when the module loads from a user-writable directory or matches the known log.dll hashes. Rationale: Uses the exact legitimate-host -> malicious-DLL pairs named in the article (BDSubWiz/bds.exe+log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder+VideoRecorderEngine.dll, GoogleDesktop+GoogleServices.dll), plus the writable paths and log.dll/BDS.exe MD5s read directly from in-article screenshot image1.jpeg (4C39087.../22AAEB49... and 28CB7B26...). Writable-path constraint removes legitimate in-product loads. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Bitdefender ConnectAgent running BDSubWiz.exe from its real Program Files path (excluded by writable-path filter)
  • Visual Studio test runs loading VideoRecorderEngine.dll from the VS install directory
  • A legacy Google Desktop install in Program Files loading GoogleServices.dll
  • Security testing/EDR validation copying these binaries into a sandbox temp folder
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loaded DLL hash against the known IOCs and verify the host binary is running from Users\Public/Temp/vss rather than its vendor install path; check the DLL export (LogInit) and ConfuserEx markers. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the DLL and host binary, kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: from the host process, pivot to child Chromium launches with --remote-debugging-port and outbound connections to *.googleapis.com; sweep fleet for the same DLL hashes and the KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe") and FileName =~ "log.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and FileName =~ "Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "GoogleDesktop.exe" and FileName =~ "GoogleServices.dll")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\vss\")
     or MD5 in~ ("4C39087E5229A70F0215AFB8B7083091","22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, Dll=FileName, DllPath=FolderPath, MD5, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Windows\vss\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Umbrij command-line switches (-deepsearch / -runas-currentuser / -debugport / -domainAd / -savepdf) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the Umbrij tool by its distinctive command-line parameters documented in the article, including the example invocation of a renamed BDSubWiz.exe with -regex and -deepsearch. These switch names are unique to Umbrij. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim Umbrij CLI parameters enumerated in the article's parameter table (-deepsearch, -runas-currentuser, -domainAd, -savepdf, -debugport, -browser). These switch spellings are tool-specific and not used by mainstream software, giving very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
ATT&CKT1528 T1134.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A bespoke internal automation tool that happens to use a -debugport plus -browser flag combination
  • Red-team replaying Umbrij invocations during an authorized engagement
  • An unrelated CLI utility using the generic -savepdf flag (mitigated by requiring the ToddyCat-specific switch set)
  • Developer testing of a custom .NET tool with similar argument naming
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the executing binary; resolve which browser/path/port were targeted (-path, -browser, -debugport) and whether -runas-currentuser/-user indicates token impersonation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and revoke/rotate the affected user's Google OAuth sessions and tokens immediately. 3) Hunt: correlate with the parent sideload host (BDS.exe/log.dll), Chromium --remote-debugging-port launches, and outbound *.googleapis.com traffic on the same host and account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "-debugport" and ProcessCommandLine has "-browser")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("-deepsearch","-runas-currentuser","-domainAd","-savepdf")
   or (CommandLine has "-debugport" and CommandLine has "-browser")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Chromium browser launched headless with --remote-debugging-port by a non-browser parent (STRD) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core Shadow-Token-via-Remote-Debug step: Umbrij launches Chrome/Edge/Chromium with a remote debugging port (often headless) to drive the user's live Gmail session. Flags browser processes carrying --remote-debugging-port when spawned by the sideload hosts or run headless. Rationale: Built on the article's explicit description of launching a Chromium browser in headless mode and connecting via the remote debugging port; pairs the --remote-debugging-port flag with the article-specific sideload parents or the --headless evasion flag to suppress legitimate interactive debugging. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1185 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers/QA running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright automation with --remote-debugging-port and --headless
  • CI build agents driving headless Chrome for screenshot or PDF generation
  • VS Code / IDE debugging a web app via the Chrome DevTools Protocol
  • Synthetic monitoring agents launching headless browsers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft VS Code" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","devenv.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and folder — a CI/automation tool from a dev path is likely benign; a browser spawned by BDSubWiz/bds/GoogleDesktop or from Users\Public/Temp is malicious. Note the --remote-debugging-port value and target profile. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the browser and parent, and immediately revoke the user's Google sessions/refresh tokens and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com connections from the same host/account and to the Umbrij CLI-switch and log.dll sideload detections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","chromium.exe","brave.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\chrome.exe", @"\msedge.exe", @"\chromium.exe", @"\brave.exe")
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\BDSubWiz.exe", @"\bds.exe", @"\VSTestVideoRecorder.exe", @"\GoogleDesktop.exe")
     or CommandLine has "--headless"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Sideload-host binary connecting to Google OAuth/Gmail API endpoints (token exchange) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access/exfil step where Umbrij (running as a renamed signed binary, not a browser) exchanges the stolen OAuth authorization code for an access token and pulls Gmail via the Google API. Flags the sideload hosts contacting *.googleapis.com / accounts.google.com. Rationale: Combines the article's OAuth-code-to-access-token exchange and Google-API access with the sideload host names confirmed in screenshot image1.jpeg; a renamed Bitdefender/VSTest/GoogleDesktop binary speaking directly to Google OAuth/Gmail APIs (work normally done only by the browser) is a strong, low-FP anomaly. Sentinel left empty because process-attributed network telemetry to these hosts is not available in standard Sentinel tables (would require Sysmon EID3 ingestion). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/ • https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2026/06/16200713/image1.jpeg • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0228/
ATT&CKT1528 T1114.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Google Desktop legacy install (in Program Files) performing update/sync checks to googleapis.com
  • Bitdefender ConnectAgent telemetry/update traffic to a Google-hosted CDN (rare; mitigated by host-name + writable-path context)
  • Security testing of the binaries in a lab with live internet
  • A renamed-but-benign internal tool reusing one of these file names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary path/signer and verify it is the renamed sideload host rather than the genuine vendor product; pull the destination URLs and timing relative to any browser remote-debug launch. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the binary, and revoke the affected Google account's OAuth tokens/refresh tokens and active sessions; review Google Workspace audit logs for token grants and bulk message reads. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts where these binaries reach Google APIs, correlate with the log.dll sideload and KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp task, and check for mailbox data staged/exfiltrated.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","bds.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oauth2.googleapis.com","accounts.google.com","www.googleapis.com","gmail.googleapis.com","googleapis.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.process_hash IN ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]

AirDrop and Quick Share Flaws Let Nearby Attackers Trigger Crashes and Bypass Checks

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 7 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Two researchers have found six security flaws in AirDrop and Quick Share, the wireless features that beam files between nearby devices with no cables or shared network. An attacker within wireless range, with just a laptop and no prior connection, can crash the sharing service on a Mac or iPhone set to receive from anyone, with no tap or prompt. The same research found Quick Share flaws that
