Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) spawning shell or LOLBin — UAF code execution · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) repeated crash/restart loop — UAF DoS · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) repeated crash/restart loop — UAF DoS AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the Google Quick Share for Windows client (nearby_share.exe) crashing and restarting repeatedly on a single host, consistent with a nearby/same-LAN attacker repeatedly colliding two connections to trigger the use-after-free described in the CISPA research. A persistent tray app restarting 5+ times in 10 minutes is not normal lifecycle behaviour. Rationale: Uses the concrete Windows Quick Share client binary name (nearby_share.exe, publisher Google LLC) confirmed via the SpyShelter process DB, plus the article's claim of a crash triggered when two connections collide. A persistent tray app restarting 5+ times / crashing repeatedly is the observable footprint of the local UAF DoS. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/apple-airdrop-google-samsung-quick-share-vulnerabilities/ • https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26967v1 • https://www.spyshelter.com/exe/google-llc-nearby_share-exe/
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine app instability after a Windows feature update or a corrupt Quick Share install causing repeated WER crashes
  • User repeatedly relaunching Quick Share manually from the system tray after it hangs on a large legitimate transfer
  • Quick Share auto-update mid-session restarting the client process several times
  • Driver/Wi-Fi adapter resets on the host destabilising the Bluetooth+Wi-Fi stack Quick Share depends on
  • Sysmon/Defender double-reporting the same process start during high event volume
Suppression filter
// Suppress benign updater-driven restarts
| where SampleFolder !has "\\Update\\" and SampleCompany has_any ("Google", "")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host actually has Quick Share for Windows installed and pull the bin(10m) of nearby_share.exe starts / Application Error 1000 events; check whether the device was in a crowded shared space (airport/conference/office Wi-Fi) at crash time and whether CFG is enforced on the binary. 2) CONTAIN: Have the user close Quick Share and set visibility off 'Everyone' (out of receive mode); if the crash loop persists, isolate the host's Wi-Fi/Bluetooth or network-isolate and ensure the Google-patched Quick Share build is installed. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC 'nearby_share.exe spawning a shell/LOLBin' on the same host/time window to rule out the crash being escalated to code execution, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the inbound peer IP that preceded the crashes.
// Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) crash-restart loop — sustained proximity/LAN UAF DoS
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where FileName =~ "nearby_share.exe"
| summarize LaunchCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleFolder = any(FolderPath), SampleCompany = any(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
        by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where LaunchCount >= 5   // >=5 (re)starts of the Quick Share tray app in 10 min = crash loop; normal lifecycle is 1 start per logon
| order by LastSeen desc
// Application Error (Event ID 1000) faulting on nearby_share.exe (Quick Share for Windows)
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventLog == "Application"
| where Source == "Application Error" and EventID == 1000
| where RenderedDescription has "nearby_share.exe"
| summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleDescription = any(RenderedDescription)
        by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CrashCount >= 3   // >=3 app-error crashes of Quick Share in 10 min
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\nearby_share.exe OR *\\Nearby_Share.exe OR *\\NEARBY_SHARE.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\nearby_share\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count())
| count >= 5
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where count>=5
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="nearby_share.exe" by Processes.dest, Processes.user, _time span=10m

Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) spawning shell or LOLBin — UAF code execution AIExploitation High
Hunts for the Quick Share for Windows client (nearby_share.exe) spawning a command shell, scripting host, or download-capable LOLBin as a child. The CISPA research notes the Windows use-after-free is plausibly exploitable for code execution because Control Flow Guard is disabled in the app; nearby_share.exe legitimately spawns no such children, so any is high-fidelity. Rationale: Grounded in the article's specific claim that the Windows Quick Share UAF is plausibly exploitable for code execution (CFG off). Uses the concrete parent binary nearby_share.exe; this tray app has no legitimate reason to spawn cmd/powershell/mshta/rundll32 etc., making the parent->child pair high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/apple-airdrop-google-samsung-quick-share-vulnerabilities/ • https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26967v1 • https://www.spyshelter.com/exe/google-llc-nearby_share-exe/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Quick Share updater logic shelling out to a maintenance/cleanup script during an in-place upgrade
  • Enterprise software-management agent injecting a child process under nearby_share.exe for inventory
  • Security tooling (EDR/DLP) reparenting or hollowing nearby_share.exe causing an apparent child spawn
  • An IT helpdesk troubleshooting script launched while Quick Share happened to be the foreground process (rare reparent)
Suppression filter
// Drop known updater path if it legitimately invokes cmd in your environment
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Quick Share\\Update\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 — decode any encoded/obfuscated args, check the child's network connections and file writes, and confirm whether a Quick Share crash (UC1) or an inbound peer connection immediately preceded this on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and capture nearby_share.exe memory; block the child binary hash if attacker-supplied. 3) HUNT: Sweep the fleet for the same parent->child pair, pivot on the child's C2 destinations across DeviceNetworkEvents, and verify all endpoints run Google's patched Quick Share build.
// nearby_share.exe (Quick Share for Windows) spawning a shell/LOLBin child — possible UAF -> code execution
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nearby_share.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// 4688: nearby_share.exe spawning shell/LOLBin
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\nearby_share.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1204.002

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

New BioShocking Attack Tricks AI Browsers Into Leaking User Credentials

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 6 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Convince an AI browser that it is playing a game, and it can hand over your login details. That is the finding behind&nbsp;BioShocking, a technique from security firm LayerX that tricked six AI browsers and assistants into copying a user's credentials and sending them to an attacker. The targets included OpenAI's ChatGPT Atlas, Perplexity's Comet, and Anthropic's Claude browser extension. An

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

ImFileEvent

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Progress Kemp LoadMaster Flaw Could Let Attackers Run Root Commands Pre-Auth

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 12 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A critical vulnerability in Progress Kemp LoadMaster can let an unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary commands as root on the appliance by sending a crafted request to its API. The flaw, tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-8037, carries a CVSS score of&nbsp;9.8 according to ZDI. A patch is available. If you run LoadMaster with the API enabled, update now. Progress&nbsp;published its advisory on June

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-33691 WAF bypass via whitespace-padded upload filename extension · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-8037 pre-auth RCE via /accessv2 heap-overflow command injection · [LLM] Root command execution on Kemp LoadMaster appliance following /accessv2 exploitation · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-8037 pre-auth RCE via /accessv2 heap-overflow command injection AIExploitation High
Hunts the watchTowr PoC payload shape for CVE-2026-8037: an unauthenticated POST to the LoadMaster /accessv2 API endpoint whose JSON body sprays many extra keys (g0..g60) each carrying a '; <cmd> # shell-injection string plus a 16-byte 'AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA' padding prefix and an apiuser value of four single quotes. This is the exact initial-access signature against an internet-facing appliance, not a generic web-attack template. Rationale: Grounded on the exact watchTowr PoC strings cross-checked from the labs.watchtowr.com write-up: endpoint /accessv2, the 16-byte 'AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA' heap-padding prefix, the '; cat /etc/passwd # injection, the g0..g60 key spray, and apiuser ''''. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty because LoadMaster is a closed Kemp appliance not enrolled in EDR/XDR or AWS; the request body lives in WAF/proxy CEF or the appliance's own syslog. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/enterprise-tech-in-shell-out-progress-kemp-loadmaster-uninitialized-heap-to-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-8037/ • https://community.progress.com/s/article/LoadMaster-Critical-Security-Bulletin-June-2026-CVE-2026-8037-CVE-2026-33691 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/progress-kemp-loadmaster-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or watchTowr 'Detection Artefact' validation firing the same payload
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) sending CVE-2026-8037 check payloads to /accessv2
  • Internal red-team exercises replaying the public PoC
  • WAF in blocking mode logging the attempt as 'denied' (true positive but already mitigated)
  • Legitimate high-volume API credential validation traffic tripping the 20-POST burst threshold during automation onboarding
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction != "blocked" and DeviceAction != "denied" and SourceIP !in ("<authorized_scanner_ips_reference_table>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the matching CommonSecurityLog rows; confirm the source IP is external/untrusted and the body contains the injection markers (g0..g60 spray, '; ... #, /etc/passwd). Check whether the WAF action was 'allowed' vs 'blocked'. 2) CONTAIN: If allowed, treat the LoadMaster as compromised at root — isolate it from the management network, block the source IP at the edge, and disable the LoadMaster API if not strictly required (per advisory). Begin emergency patch to GA v7.2.63.2 / LTSF v7.2.54.18. 3) HUNT: Pivot to the appliance's syslog (UC: root command execution) for shell activity (/etc/passwd reads, reverse shells), review LoadMaster config and SSH authorized_keys for persistence, and scope all source IPs that hit /accessv2 with these markers across the full retention window.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/accessv2"
| where Message has_any ("'; cat /etc/passwd #", "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA", "/etc/passwd", "\"g60\"", "\"apiuser\":\"''''\"")
   or RequestContext has_any ("'; cat /etc/passwd #", "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA", "/etc/passwd")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Progress Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-8037 Pre-Auth RCE Exploitation Attempt

Root command execution on Kemp LoadMaster appliance following /accessv2 exploitation AIExploitation Medium
Execution-phase confirmation for CVE-2026-8037: the injected command runs as root on the LoadMaster appliance. Hunts the appliance's forwarded syslog for shell-command execution indicators (/etc/passwd reads, /bin/sh -c, reverse-shell /dev/tcp/ or bash -i) originating from a host named like a LoadMaster, which should never legitimately spawn arbitrary shells. Rationale: Targets the article's core claim that the command 'runs as root' on the appliance. A load balancer spawning /bin/sh, reading /etc/passwd, or opening a /dev/tcp reverse shell is never legitimate, making these high-fidelity post-exploitation indicators. Empty Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch: the appliance cannot host an EDR agent — only its remote syslog is observable. Hunting tier because it depends on the appliance being configured to forward syslog and named per convention. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/enterprise-tech-in-shell-out-progress-kemp-loadmaster-uninitialized-heap-to-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-8037/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/progress-kemp-loadmaster-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kemp support/diagnostic sessions where an admin legitimately opens a root shell for troubleshooting
  • Firmware update or backup routines that touch /etc/passwd or spawn shell helpers
  • Authorized configuration scripts run by the appliance's own automation
  • Penetration test PoC replay reading /etc/passwd
  • Syslog from a non-appliance host that happens to match the 'kemp'/'loadmaster' name substring
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "kemp-support" and SeverityLevel != "debug"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the source host is genuinely the LoadMaster appliance and that the shell activity has no matching authorized admin/maintenance window; correlate the timestamp against /accessv2 POST hits (UC1) within the preceding minutes. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, isolate the appliance from management and production networks, capture a config/state snapshot for forensics, and rotate any credentials/keys stored on or reachable from the appliance. 3) HUNT: Enumerate persistence — SSH authorized_keys under /root, cron/systemd entries, modified LoadMaster config — and review egress firewall logs for outbound connections initiated by the appliance IP (reverse shell / tooling download).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Computer has_any ("loadmaster", "lmos", "kemp") or HostName has_any ("loadmaster", "lmos", "kemp")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/dev/tcp/", "bash -i", "/bin/sh -c", "/bin/bash -c", "; cat ", "| sh")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, SeverityLevel, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (@host.name:(*loadmaster* OR *LoadMaster* OR *lmos* OR *kemp* OR *Kemp*)) AND ("/etc/passwd" OR "/dev/tcp/" OR "bash -i" OR "/bin/sh -c" OR "/bin/bash -c")
WEB
index=* sourcetype=syslog (host=*loadmaster* OR host=*lmos* OR host=*kemp*) ("/etc/passwd" OR "/dev/tcp/" OR "bash -i" OR "/bin/sh -c" OR "/bin/bash -c")
| table _time host process syslog_message
| sort - _time
| comment("LoadMaster forwards to a non-CIM syslog sourcetype; raw search. Scope host to your appliance naming convention.")
Kemp LoadMaster CVE-2026-33691 WAF bypass via whitespace-padded upload filename extension AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the second patched flaw in the same advisory: a WAF/upload extension-check bypass where whitespace padding around a filename extension (e.g. evil.php<space> or evil .php / %20.php) slips a disallowed file type past the filter. Detects upload requests to LoadMaster whose filename contains whitespace adjacent to an executable/script extension. Rationale: Grounded on the advisory's description of CVE-2026-33691 — 'whitespace padding in filenames could circumvent file upload extension checks.' Matches whitespace immediately adjacent to a script/executable extension in the upload filename or URL-encoded path, a pattern legitimate uploads almost never produce. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: appliance upload telemetry lives only in the front-end WAF/proxy, not in endpoint EDR or AWS. Cross-checked against: • https://community.progress.com/s/article/LoadMaster-Critical-Security-Bulletin-June-2026-CVE-2026-8037-CVE-2026-33691 • https://securityonline.info/kemp-loadmaster-vulnerabilities-waf-bypass-os-injection/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/progress-kemp-loadmaster-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1036.008
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user uploading a legitimately named file that happens to contain a trailing space before a known extension
  • Document-management workflows that rename files with padded extensions
  • Automated tooling that URL-encodes spaces (%20) in legitimate filenames
  • Security scanner testing upload filters with whitespace mutation payloads
  • Double-extension business files (e.g. report.tar .gz) tripping the regex
Suppression filter
| where FileName !endswith " .gz" and FileName !endswith " .bz2" and SourceIP !in ("<authorized_scanner_ips_reference_table>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the captured filename and upload endpoint; confirm the whitespace is adjacent to an executable/script extension (.php/.cgi/.sh) rather than a benign document type, and identify the resulting stored path. 2) CONTAIN: If a script/webshell-capable file was accepted, quarantine it on the appliance, block the source IP, and confirm the appliance is patched to GA v7.2.63.2 / LTSF v7.2.54.18. 3) HUNT: Search appliance syslog for subsequent execution of the uploaded path, review web logs for requests back to the uploaded filename (webshell interaction), and scope all sources that submitted whitespace-padded upload filenames.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST" or RequestMethod =~ "PUT" or isempty(RequestMethod)
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)\s+\.(php|cgi|sh|pl|jsp|asp|aspx|exe)\b"
    or FileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(php|cgi|sh|pl|jsp|asp|aspx|exe)\s+$"
    or RequestURL has_any ("%20.php", "%20.cgi", "%20.sh", ".php%20", ".cgi%20")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, FileName, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| where Account !endswith "$"

Oracle E-Business Suite Flaw CVE-2026-46817 Actively Exploited in the Wild

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 13 use cases 5 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A critical security flaw impacting Oracle E-Business Suite has come under active exploitation in the wild, according to Defused Cyber. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-46817 (CVSS score: 9.8), refers to an improper privilege management and authentication flaw in Oracle Payments that could be abused to take over susceptible instances. "Easily exploitable vulnerability allows

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Exposure: internet-facing Oracle EBS Payments 12.2.3-12.2.15 unpatched for CVE-2026-46817 · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound connections from Oracle EBS CVE-2026-46817 actor IP 45.84.137.125 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Oracle EBS iPayment ibytransmit path-traversal exploit (CVE-2026-46817) reading /etc/passwd · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Oracle EBS iPayment ibytransmit path-traversal exploit (CVE-2026-46817) reading /etc/passwd AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests to the Oracle iPayment file-transmission endpoint /OA_HTML/ibytransmit carrying the CODEX_PULL / FULL_FILE_PATH path-traversal payload used to exfiltrate /etc/passwd. This is the exact in-the-wild exploitation pattern for CVE-2026-46817 captured on Defused Cyber honeypots, not a generic web-exploit template. Rationale: Anchors on the obscure Oracle iPayment endpoint /OA_HTML/ibytransmit plus the CODEX_PULL/FULL_FILE_PATH/etc-passwd payload strings confirmed across BleepingComputer, Help Net Security, SecurityWeek and Rescana write-ups of the same honeypot capture — this endpoint sees near-zero legitimate external POST traffic, making it high-fidelity. Defender KQL left empty: Defender XDR does not ingest inbound HTTP request URIs/bodies for server processes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-oracle-e-business-suite-flaw-now-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/oracle-payments-cve-2026-46817-exploitation/ • https://www.securityweek.com/exploitation-of-recent-oracle-e-business-suite-vulnerability-begins/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-critical-oracle-e-business-suite-cve-2026-46817-vulnerability-targeting-oracle-payments-module
ATT&CKT1190 T1003.008 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate B2B payment partner integrations that genuinely use the iPayment ibytransmit file-transmission interface
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Nessus, Qualys) probing the EBS endpoint during scheduled scans
  • Internal red-team / pentest validation of CVE-2026-46817
  • Oracle support or DBA diagnostics hitting the endpoint from a known jump host
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)) and UserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","Tenable")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the matched event and check whether the XML body contains CODEX_PULL with FULL_FILE_PATH=/etc/passwd, and whether HttpStatusCode == 200 (successful file read). Reputation-check the SrcIpAddr (45.84.137.125 / AS136787 PacketHub is the known actor). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge and, if a 200 with file-read payload is confirmed, isolate the EBS web tier and rotate any OS/app credentials exposed via /etc/passwd-adjacent reads. 3) Hunt: review web logs for other POSTs to /OA_HTML/* from the same IP, look for webshell drops in the OA_HTML doc root, and check for new outbound connections or interactive shells from the EBS host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "/OA_HTML/ibytransmit"
| extend PayloadHit = Url has_any ("CODEX_PULL","FULL_FILE_PATH","/etc/passwd","DeliveryRequest")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, PayloadHit
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound connections from Oracle EBS CVE-2026-46817 actor IP 45.84.137.125 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts any network connection from the confirmed CVE-2026-46817 exploitation source IP 45.84.137.125 (AS136787 PacketHub, France) to internet-facing Oracle E-Business Suite hosts on 443. A pure IOC pivot that catches the actor even when WAF/web-log payload telemetry is missing. Rationale: 45.84.137.125 is the single confirmed actor IP from the Defused honeypot capture, cross-validated by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek; an external IP-only match against EBS hosts is low-volume and high-fidelity for this specific campaign. Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: the EBS web tier is a Linux server whose firewall/flow telemetry does not map to the standard Datadog or CloudWatch sources in scope. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-oracle-e-business-suite-flaw-now-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://www.securityweek.com/exploitation-of-recent-oracle-e-business-suite-vulnerability-begins/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-critical-oracle-e-business-suite-cve-2026-46817-vulnerability-targeting-oracle-payments-module

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed validation / sandbox detonation traffic sourced from the same hosting range
  • Security researcher or scanner sharing the AS136787 PacketHub egress range
  • Stale NAT/proxy reuse if the IP is later reassigned to a benign tenant
  • An analyst manually curl-testing the IOC from a corporate egress that the IP happens to also use
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DstHostname/DeviceName is an internet-facing Oracle EBS host and correlate the connection time with any /OA_HTML/ibytransmit POSTs in web logs. 2) Contain: block 45.84.137.125 (and consider the AS136787 PacketHub range) at the perimeter firewall and WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot on the destination host for successful 200 responses on iPayment endpoints, new files in the OA_HTML doc root, and any outbound beaconing from the EBS host post-connection.

Exposure: internet-facing Oracle EBS Payments 12.2.3-12.2.15 unpatched for CVE-2026-46817 AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces Oracle E-Business Suite hosts carrying CVE-2026-46817 (Oracle Payments, versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15) so the SOC can prioritise the May 2026 CSPU patch on internet-facing instances before opportunistic exploitation. Exposure-reduction hunt tied to the actively exploited CVE. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-46817) and affected version band (12.2.3-12.2.15) named by NVD/The Hacker News and confirmed actively exploited; joining TVM to IsInternetFacing prioritises the exact hosts the actor can reach. Sigma omitted (posture/exposure query, not a single-event detection); Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch omitted (no vulnerability-inventory event in those schemas). Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-46817 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/oracle-e-business-suite-flaw-cve-2026.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/oracle-payments-cve-2026-46817-exploitation/

Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Internal-only EBS instances flagged as exposure but not actually reachable from the internet
  • Decommissioned/test EBS servers still reporting to TVM
  • Version banner mismatch where a compensating WAF virtual-patch is already in place
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort results by IsInternetFacing and confirm each host's actual internet reachability and current EBS patch level against the May 2026 CSPU. 2) Contain: virtual-patch internet-facing unpatched hosts at the WAF (block /OA_HTML/ibytransmit) and schedule emergency patching. 3) Hunt: for any host that was internet-facing and unpatched during the exploitation window, retro-hunt web logs for /OA_HTML/ibytransmit POSTs and connections from 45.84.137.125.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-29 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious Chromium-based extension that spoofs the AI-powered answer engine Perplexity AI redirects browser search traffic using MV3 APIs and intermediary infrastructure. The post Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1566
Domainsperplexity-ai.online oda.digital extension.tilda.ws

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious Perplexity-spoofing extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to disk · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Search-interception traffic to Perplexity typosquat domain perplexity-ai[.]online · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Search-interception traffic to Perplexity typosquat domain perplexity-ai[.]online AICommand & Control High
Hunts browser connections/DNS resolutions to the attacker-controlled search-interception infrastructure (perplexity-ai.online and related oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws) used by the fake 'Search for perplexity ai' Chromium extension. Because the extension routes every Omnibox query and keystroke-level suggestion through this domain before redirecting to a real engine, any browser-originated traffic to these hosts is high-fidelity evidence of an infected endpoint. Rationale: Anchored on the exact interception domain perplexity-ai.online (confirmed by both the MSFT blog and The Hacker News) plus the pre-extracted secondary infra oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws, scoped to browser parent processes — a typosquat domain reached by a browser is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/search-for-perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd • https://www.crx4chrome.com/extensions/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176 T1185
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/IR analyst detonating the extension sample in a managed sandbox host
  • Web proxy / secure-web-gateway pre-fetching or URL-categorizing the domain on a user's behalf
  • Threat-intel enrichment or DNS-sinkhole tooling resolving the IOC for blocking
  • A user who clicked the lookalike landing page once but did not install (single browse vs. repeated query routing)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which device/user generated the traffic and whether the 'Search for perplexity ai' extension (ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd) is installed; check if default search provider was overridden to perplexity-ai.online. 2) Contain: force-remove the extension via browser policy/ExtensionInstallBlocklist, reset the default search engine, and block perplexity-ai.online / oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws at proxy and DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on all other hosts resolving these domains and review browsing/search history routed through the domain for sensitive query exposure during the exposure window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","chrome_proxy.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious Perplexity-spoofing extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to disk AIInstallation High
Hunts for the unique Chrome Web Store extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd ('Search for perplexity ai') appearing in browser extension folder paths or written files on managed endpoints. The extension ID is a globally unique 32-char identifier, so any file-system artifact bearing it is a deterministic indicator that the taken-down malicious search hijacker was installed. Rationale: The 32-char extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd is a globally unique store identifier (confirmed via the Chrome Web Store and crx4chrome listings), so its presence in any extension folder path is a deterministic install indicator with effectively no collisions. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/search-for-perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd • https://www.crx4chrome.com/extensions/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd/
ATT&CKT1176 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup software capturing the Chrome 'User Data' profile directory that still contains the extension folder
  • IR/forensic collection tooling copying browser profiles for offline analysis
  • AV/EDR scanning or quarantining the extension folder (file-access touches the path)
  • Sync of an already-infected profile to a new device via Chrome profile sync before takedown
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the ActionType (FileCreated = fresh install vs FileDeleted = remediation) and identify the user profile and browser hosting the extension folder. 2) Contain: remove the extension, push it to the browser ExtensionInstallBlocklist policy, and reset the hijacked default search provider; block perplexity-ai.online at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 network telemetry to confirm queries were exfiltrated, and sweep the fleet for the same extension ID to find all installs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
